usage: I look up / look at the top
examples: 책상 위에 컴퓨터가 있어요.
There is a computer on the desk.
Basic frame: noun 위에 + 있다 says where a thing sits.
고양이가 지붕 위에서 자요.
The cat is sleeping on the roof.
에서 (not 에) because sleeping is an action happening up there.
손을 머리 위로 올리세요.
Raise your hands above your head.
위로 with 로 shows movement toward the top, used in real instructions.
nuance: 위 (Sino-Korean would be 上, but 위 is native Korean) names the top surface of something or the space directly above it, and it must attach to a noun: 책상 위, 머리 위, never standing alone like English 'up'. The closest confusable is 위쪽: 위 points at the top itself or 'on top of', while 위쪽 means 'the upper side/upward direction' more loosely (방 위쪽이 더워요 = the upper part of the room is hotter). It is neutral in register and used by everyone, all day, for both physical position (책상 위) and abstract rank (위 사람 = a superior). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 위 like a preposition and dropping the noun, or saying 위에서 있어요 for simple existence — existence takes 에 (위에 있어요), and 에서 is reserved for an action done up there. Also do not confuse the noun 위 with 위 meaning 'stomach' (a different word, 한자 胃); context and the attached noun keep them apart.

mistakes: Saying 위에서 있어요 for 'it is on top' — existence uses 에 (위에 있어요); 에서 only marks where an action happens.
Dropping the noun and using 위 like English 'up' (위에 가요 to mean 'go up') — you need a noun (계단 위에 = on top of the stairs) or a motion verb like 올라가요.
Mixing up positional 위 with 위 = 'stomach' (위가 아파요 = my stomach hurts); the standalone meaning depends entirely on context.

examples: 의자 아래에 가방이 있어요.
There is a bag under the chair.
Basic frame: noun 아래에 + 있다 locates the bag.
아이들이 나무 아래에서 놀아요.
The children are playing under the tree.
에서 because playing is an action carried out in that shaded spot.
사인은 이 줄 아래에 해 주세요.
Please sign below this line.
Everyday paperwork use: 아래에 = on the lower side / below.
nuance: 아래 is the native Korean word for the area below or underneath something, and like all position nouns it clings to a noun: 책상 아래, 다리 아래. Its near-twin is 밑, and the boundary matters: 아래 is the broader 'below / lower area' (and can be abstract — 평균 아래 = below average), while 밑 leans more concrete and tactile, 'right underneath, the underside' (책상 밑에 = right under the desk, often where you'd reach with your hand), and 밑 sounds a touch more casual. 아래 also contrasts with 아래쪽 ('the lower side / downward direction', vaguer). Register is neutral; everyone uses it. English speakers stumble in three ways: using 밑 and 아래 as if identical (usually fine, but 밑 is more physical and informal), saying 아래에서 있어요 for plain existence (it should be 아래에 있어요), and forgetting that 아래 is a noun, so 'go down' is not 아래 가요 but 아래로 내려가요 with a motion verb.

usage: it is in front of the door
I meet in front of the station
examples: 학교 앞에 편의점이 있어요.
There is a convenience store in front of the school.
Basic frame: noun 앞에 + 있다 places the store.
카페 앞에서 친구를 기다려요.
I wait for my friend in front of the cafe.
에서 because waiting is an action you do at that spot.
회의를 앞두고 자료를 준비해요.
I prepare materials ahead of the meeting.
앞 also means 'ahead in time' — 앞두다 takes an object (회의를 앞두다) = to have an event coming up.
nuance: 앞 is the native Korean noun for the front side of a thing or the space directly ahead of it, and it attaches to a noun: 집 앞, 역 앞. Crucially, 앞 covers BOTH space ('in front of') and time ('ahead, upcoming') — 앞으로 means 'from now on / going forward', and 앞두다 means an event is just ahead. Compare it with 정면 (the literal 'front face/facade', more formal and architectural) and with 앞쪽 ('the front side/forward direction', vaguer). It is neutral in register. The big English-speaker traps: (1) saying 앞에서 있어요 for existence instead of 앞에 있어요; (2) over-relying on the spatial sense and missing the temporal one, so 앞으로 gets misread as a place; and (3) confusing 앞 with the direction word 앞으로 — 앞 alone is the noun (a location), while 앞으로 adds 로/으로 to mean 'toward the front / henceforth'. Remember it is a noun, so 'go forward' is 앞으로 가다, not 앞 가다.

examples: 건물 뒤에 주차장이 있어요.
There is a parking lot behind the building.
Basic frame: noun 뒤에 + 있다 places the lot.
줄 뒤에서 차례를 기다려요.
I wait my turn at the back of the line.
에서 because waiting is an action you perform there.
이 일은 뒤에 다시 이야기해요.
Let's talk about this matter later.
뒤 can also mean 'later/afterward' in time, not only physical space.
nuance: 뒤 is the native Korean noun for the back side of something or the space behind it, and it attaches to a noun: 집 뒤, 건물 뒤. Like 앞, it spans space AND time: 뒤에 can mean 'behind' (place) or 'later / afterward' (time, e.g. 그 뒤에 = after that). The most dangerous confusable for learners is the Sino-Korean 후 (後): 후 is purely temporal ('after', as in 식사 후 = after the meal), so 'after class' is 수업 후 / 수업 뒤(에), but a parking lot is only 건물 뒤, never 건물 후. Also contrast 뒤쪽 ('the rear side/backward direction', vaguer). Register is neutral. usage: it is next to the bank
I wait next to the station
examples: 창문 옆에 책상이 있어요.
There is a desk next to the window.
Basic frame: noun 옆에 + 있다 places the desk.
카페 옆에서 버스를 타요.
I catch the bus next to the cafe.
에서 because catching the bus is an action done at that spot.
바로 옆집에 사촌이 살아요.
My cousin lives right next door.
옆 compounds into 옆집 (the house beside) — a natural everyday word.
nuance: 옆 is the native Korean noun for the side of a thing or the spot immediately beside it, and it attaches to a noun: 창문 옆, 은행 옆. It implies adjacency — right alongside, within touching or glancing distance — unlike 근처 ('in the vicinity', possibly some distance away) or 옆쪽 ('the side direction', vaguer). It also forms handy compounds: 옆집 (the house next door), 옆자리 (the seat beside you), 옆사람 (the person next to you). Register is neutral and very high-frequency in daily speech. The English-speaker traps: (1) 옆에서 있어요 for existence rather than 옆에 있어요; (2) reaching for 옆 when the thing is merely 'in the area' — that is 근처, while 옆 is strictly 'right next to'; and (3) forgetting the noun requirement, so 'sit beside me' is 제 옆에 앉으세요 (literally 'sit at my side'), not a bare preposition. Note 옆 is also written/pronounced carefully: the ㅍ batchim links to following vowels (옆에 sounds like '여페').

Forgetting 옆 is a noun and needs a possessor/noun before it — 'next to me' is 제 옆에, not just 옆에 floating alone.

examples: 가방 안에 열쇠가 있어요.
There is a key inside the bag.
Basic frame: noun 안에 + 있다 says the key is enclosed.
방 안에서 음악을 들어요.
I listen to music inside the room.
에서 because listening is an action done within that space.
이건 예산 안에서 해결해요.
Let's handle this within the budget.
안 also marks abstract limits: 'within' a budget, rule, or range.
nuance: 안 is the native Korean noun for the inside or interior of an enclosed space, attaching to a noun: 가방 안, 방 안. Beyond physical interiors it marks LIMITS — 'within' a time or range: 한 시간 안에 (within an hour), 예산 안에서 (within budget). Two confusables matter. First, 속: both mean 'inside', but 속 implies being buried/immersed in a mass or depth (물속 = underwater, 마음속 = deep in one's heart, 가방 속 = down in the bag's contents), while 안 is the plainer 'inside the boundary' (방 안 = in the room). Second, the homograph 안 = 'not' (the negation adverb, 안 가요 = I don't go) — same syllable, totally different word, told apart by position (a negating 안 sits before a verb; the noun 안 follows a noun). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping 안 and using bare 에, so 가방에 넣어요 ('put it to/at the bag') instead of the clearer 가방 안에 넣어요 ('put it inside the bag'); (2) overusing 속 where plain 안 is natural; and (3) saying 안에서 있어요 for existence instead of 안에 있어요.

mistakes: Saying 가방에 instead of 가방 안에 when you specifically mean 'inside it' — bare 에 is just 'at/to the bag'; add 안 to say within.
Confusing the noun 안 (inside) with the adverb 안 (not): 안 가요 means 'I don't go', while 방 안 means 'inside the room' — position before/after a verb tells you which.
Using 속 everywhere for 'inside' — 속 implies depth/immersion (마음속, 물속); for a plain enclosed space use 안 (방 안에).

examples: 문 밖에 택배가 있어요.
There is a parcel outside the door.
Basic frame: noun 밖에 + 있다 locates the parcel.
날씨가 좋아서 밖에서 점심을 먹어요.
The weather is nice, so I eat lunch outside.
에서 because eating is an action done out there.
저는 밖에 잘 안 나가요.
I don't really go out much.
밖에 나가다 is the everyday way to say 'go out / leave the house'.
nuance: 밖 is the native Korean noun for the outside or exterior of a place, attaching to a noun: 집 밖, 문 밖. Beware a crucial homograph: 밖에 also functions as a particle meaning 'only / nothing but', and it then REQUIRES a negative verb — 하나밖에 없어요 = 'there is only one' (literally 'outside of one, none'). So 밖에 has two lives: positional noun 밖 + 에 (집 밖에 있어요 = it's outside the house) versus the limiting particle 밖에 (천 원밖에 없어요 = I only have 1000 won). You disambiguate by the verb: positional 밖에 takes a normal verb, particle 밖에 forces a negative (없어요/안). Contrast also with 바깥 (a near-synonym noun for 'outside/outdoors', slightly more concrete, as in 바깥 공기 = the outside air) and 밖쪽 ('the outer side', vaguer). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) saying 밖에서 있어요 for existence instead of 밖에 있어요; (2) being thrown by the 'only' particle 밖에 and forgetting it needs a negative; and (3) treating 밖 as a verb — 'go outside' is 밖으로 나가다 or 밖에 나가다, not 밖 가다.

usage: between the bank and the cafe
사이 + 에 with 과/와 linking both sides
examples: 은행과 카페 사이에 작은 가게가 있어요.
There is a small shop between the bank and the cafe.
Basic frame: A와/과 B 사이에 + 있다 places the shop between two named things.
건물 사이에서 바람이 불어요.
Wind blows between the buildings.
에서 because the wind blowing is an action occurring in that gap.
두 사람 사이가 점점 가까워져요.
The two people are growing closer.
사이 also means a human relationship — 사이가 좋다/나쁘다 = get along well/badly.
nuance: 사이 is the native Korean noun for the space, gap, or interval between two things, attaching with the linking particle 와/과 to name both sides: 은행과 카페 사이, 너와 나 사이. It is wonderfully broad — physical gaps (건물 사이), time intervals (방학 사이에 = during the break), and crucially human RELATIONSHIPS (친구 사이 = the bond between friends; 사이가 좋다 = to be close). Compare it with 가운데/중간 ('the middle/center' of a single thing or group, not the gap between two distinct items): the chair in the center of the room is 방 가운데, but the shop wedged between the bank and cafe is 은행과 카페 사이. Register is neutral and idiomatic. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) dropping the 와/과 that grammatically pairs the two sides, so 은행 카페 사이 sounds unfinished — say 은행과 카페 사이; (2) using 사이 for the center of one object where 가운데 belongs; and (3) missing the relationship meaning, so 우리 사이 ('our relationship') gets misread as a physical gap. Colloquially 사이 even contracts to 새 (밤새 = all through the night).

usage: to the left of the door
it is to the left of the bank
I meet on the left of the station
examples: 문 왼쪽에 거울이 있어요.
There is a mirror to the left of the door.
Basic frame: noun 왼쪽에 + 있다 places the mirror.
가게 왼쪽에서 버스를 타요.
I catch the bus to the left of the shop.
에서 because catching the bus is an action done at that spot.
사거리에서 왼쪽으로 가세요.
Turn left at the intersection.
왼쪽으로 with 으로 gives real walking/driving directions.
nuance: 왼쪽 is the native compound noun for the left side or leftward direction, built from 왼- ('left') + 쪽 ('side/direction'); it attaches to a noun (문 왼쪽) or stands with a direction particle for movement (왼쪽으로 = to the left). The -쪽 element is the same one in 위쪽/아래쪽/앞쪽, marking 'the ~ side'. Its direct opposite is 오른쪽 (right), and confusing the two is the single most common error when giving directions — practice the pair until 왼 reliably means left. Note also the more formal/literary 좌 (左, Sino-Korean) seen in 좌회전 (left turn, on road signs) versus everyday spoken 왼쪽. Register: 왼쪽 is the normal conversational word; 좌 appears in fixed/official terms. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 왼쪽에서 있어요 for existence instead of 왼쪽에 있어요; (2) swapping 왼쪽 and 오른쪽 under pressure; and (3) using 왼쪽 alone for 'turn left' (왼쪽 도세요 is incomplete) — you need the direction particle: 왼쪽으로 도세요 / 왼쪽으로 가세요.

usage: to the right of the door
it is to the right of the cafe
I wait on the right of the station
examples: 카페 오른쪽에 은행이 있어요.
There is a bank to the right of the cafe.
Basic frame: noun 오른쪽에 + 있다 places the bank.
건물 오른쪽에서 친구를 만나요.
I meet my friend to the right of the building.
에서 because meeting is an action done at that spot.
다음 신호에서 오른쪽으로 가세요.
Go right at the next light.
오른쪽으로 with 으로 is how real directions are spoken.
nuance: 오른쪽 is the native compound noun for the right side or rightward direction, from 오른- ('right') + 쪽 ('side/direction'); it attaches to a noun (문 오른쪽) or pairs with a direction particle for motion (오른쪽으로 = to the right). The formal/Sino-Korean counterpart is 우 (右), found in signage like 우회전 (right turn) and the set phrase 좌우 (左右, left-and-right), while 오른쪽 is the everyday spoken form. Register: 오른쪽 is conversational, 우 is official/written. examples: 집 근처에 큰 공원이 있어요.
There is a big park near my house.
Basic frame: noun 근처에 + 있다 places the park in the area.
역 근처에서 친구를 만나요.
I meet my friend near the station.
에서 because meeting is an action done in that vicinity.
이 근처에 약국 있어요?
Is there a pharmacy around here?
이 근처 (around here) is the phrase travelers use to ask for nearby places.
nuance: 근처 is a Sino-Korean noun (近處, 近 'near' + 處 'place') meaning the nearby area or vicinity surrounding a place; it attaches to a noun (집 근처) or to 이/그/저 (이 근처 = around here). Unlike the adjacency word 옆 ('right next to', touching distance), 근처 covers a looser radius — a few minutes' walk, the general neighborhood. Two near-synonyms to weigh: 근방 (近方) is a slightly more colloquial 'thereabouts', and 부근 (附近) is a more formal/written 'vicinity' (역 부근 sounds bookish); 근처 is the neutral everyday default. Compare also 가까이 (an adverb, 'nearby/closely', as in 가까이 오세요 = come closer) — 근처 is a place noun, 가까이 modifies a verb. Register: 근처 is comfortably conversational. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 근처에서 있어요 for existence instead of 근처에 있어요; (2) using 근처 when the thing is literally adjacent, where 옆 is sharper; and (3) confusing the noun 근처 with the adverb 가까이 — say 집 근처에 있어요 (noun), but 가까이 사세요? for 'do you live nearby?' with the adverbial feel.

usage: in the middle of the room
it is in the middle of the room
I rest in the middle of the park
examples: 방 가운데에 식탁이 있어요.
There is a dining table in the middle of the room.
Basic frame: noun 가운데에 + 있다 places the table at the center.
공원 가운데에서 아이들이 놀아요.
Children play in the middle of the park.
에서 because playing is an action done in that central spot.
여러 색 가운데 파란색을 골랐어요.
Among the various colors, I chose blue.
가운데 also means 'among/out of' a set, like 셋 가운데 하나 = one of three.
nuance: 가운데 is the native Korean noun for the middle or center point of a space, and figuratively 'among' a group; it attaches to a noun (방 가운데) and can mark selection (셋 가운데 하나 = one among three). Its key confusable is 사이: 가운데 is the center of ONE object or area (방 가운데 = the middle of the room), whereas 사이 is the gap BETWEEN two distinct things (은행과 카페 사이 = between the bank and the cafe) — don't use 가운데 to mean 'between two items'. Compare also 중간 (中間, Sino-Korean 'midpoint/midway'), which overlaps but leans toward the middle of a line, range, or process (중간고사 = midterm exam, 중간에 = midway through), while 가운데 feels more like the spatial center or 'among a set'. And 중심 (中心) is the abstract 'core/focal center'. Register: 가운데 is neutral and common. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using 가운데 for 'between two things' where 사이 is correct; (2) saying 가운데에서 있어요 for existence instead of 가운데에 있어요; and (3) swapping 가운데 and 중간 carelessly — 'midway through the movie' is 영화 중간에, while 'the center of the table' is 식탁 가운데.
